# Cascade map

Shows whether an X-Matrix's annual objectives actually land on someone at the level below — which are genuinely committed, which are still just a proposal, and which nobody has picked up at all.

Family: Hoshin Kanri · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

A cascade map records the one hand-off Hoshin Kanri depends on and nothing else in this catalogue tracks: whether a parent plan's annual objectives actually became real, owned work at the level below. An X-Matrix sets one level's plan; catchball is the negotiation that produces it; a cascade map is the separate, later question of what happened to each objective after that — did a real unit take it on, and is that commitment real or just a name on a slide. It is not a KPI tree: a KPI tree breaks one goal into the driver metrics that move it, inside a single function; a cascade map tracks which unit owns which objective, across multiple units, and says nothing about the metrics that prove any of them are moving.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- You have a real X-Matrix (or a prior year's cascade) whose annual objectives need to become owned work at the level below it.
- You want an honest record of which objectives have a real, committed owner and which are still just proposed — not a plan that looks complete because every cell got filled in.
- You're checking whether the load is actually balanced across units, not quietly concentrated on the same team that always says yes.

Not when:

- You don't have a parent plan yet — build the X-Matrix first; a cascade map has nothing to cascade from without one.
- You want a single function's own goal-to-metric breakdown — that's a KPI tree, not a cascade map. A cascade map is about which unit owns which objective; a KPI tree is what that unit tracks once it does.
- You're tempted to mark a link 'committed' just to make coverage look complete — an objective assigned on paper with no real agreement behind it is exactly the failure catchball itself exists to prevent, one level up.

## How to fill it in

- **parentObjectives** — Name the parent X-Matrix and describe its real annual objectives — a first-pass list gets drafted from that, for you to correct against the plan's actual objectives and targets.
- **units** — The teams, divisions, or sites this plan needs to cascade to — drafted from your description.
- **links** — Only enter a link where a unit has actually proposed or committed to carrying a parent objective forward as its own, with a local objective that's genuinely more specific than the parent one — a real hand-off, never the parent text copied down.
- **coverage** — Computed for you from your parent objectives, units, and links — nothing to enter here.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the cascade actually built.
- **nextSteps** — What will you do about a dark objective or an unloaded unit, ranked by impact and effort, owned and dated.

## What good looks like

The example below cascades Northwind Fabrication's own FY2027 X-Matrix (the Hoshin Kanri worked example) to its shop-floor teams: two of the three annual objectives have a real, committed owner — the CNC Shop Floor and Scheduling teams — while the late-shipment objective is still only proposed to Quality, honestly left uncommitted rather than marked done to round the numbers up.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/cascade-map

## Common mistakes

- **Marking a link 'committed' when it's really still just an assignment on paper.** — A unit that was told to own an objective, but never actually agreed to it, hasn't really taken it on — the whole point of tracking 'proposed' separately is catching this before the year ends and nobody delivered.
- **Copying the parent objective's text down as the local objective instead of making it genuinely more specific.** — A cascade that doesn't get more specific at each level isn't actually cascading — it's relabeling. The local objective should say exactly what this unit is going to do, not restate the parent's aspiration.
- **Building the cascade once at the start of the year and never updating it as proposals turn into commitments or quietly fall through.** — Same living-document discipline as the X-Matrix itself — a cascade map that was accurate in January and never touched again is stale by the first business review.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **Hoshin Kanri — X-Matrix** — The parent plan this cascades from — a cascade map has nothing to track without a real X-Matrix's annual objectives behind it.

Downstream:

- **KPI tree** — Once a unit actually commits to a local objective here, a KPI tree is often what that unit builds next to track the driver metrics that move it week to week — the cascade map records the hand-off, the KPI tree is what happens after.
- **A3 problem solving** — When a committed local objective isn't moving, an A3 is the right tool to find out why — the cascade map shows who owns it, the A3 closes the specific gap.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding whether a unit has actually committed to an objective or merely been assigned it
- Deciding which dark objective or unloaded unit to chase down first

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting a first-pass parent-objective and unit list from a description of the parent plan
- Drafting the narrative from the cascade actually built

Drudgery — automated:

- Computing cascade coverage and per-unit load
- Flagging dark objectives — parent objectives with zero committed links
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
